questions.q: Per this lesson, what does centralized design buy, and what does decentralized design buy?
options: Centralized design buys speed; decentralized design buys consistency
Centralized design eliminates the need for any governance at all
Both models buy exactly the same benefits, just with different names

Centralized design buys consistency -- one team catching conflicts and enforcing one coherent data model; decentralized design buys speed -- business-unit admins shipping changes without a central review queue
questions.explain: The lesson frames the tradeoff plainly: centralization catches conflicts and enforces consistency across the whole org, at the cost of speed; decentralization lets teams move fast on their own changes, at the cost of consistency.

questions.q: What failure mode does this lesson describe for a fully centralized model that scales past what the central team can handle?
options: It becomes a bottleneck -- business units wait weeks for small changes, which produces workarounds like shadow Flows that undermine the consistency centralization was meant to protect
The model becomes cheaper to run as it scales
It automatically converts itself into a Center of Excellence model
It eliminates all naming-convention inconsistency permanently
questions.explain: The lesson calls out this bottleneck explicitly as the predictable failure mode of over-centralization, including the workaround behaviors it tends to produce.

questions.q: What is a 'Center of Excellence' (CoE) model, as described in this lesson?
options: A model where business units have zero authority and everything routes through one team

A hybrid model where a central team owns platform-wide concerns like data model standards and security architecture, while business units retain real authority to build their own team-specific work within those guardrails
A separate Salesforce org created exclusively for training purposes
A certification Salesforce awards to orgs with more than 1,000 users
questions.explain: A CoE is framed as a genuine resolution, not a watered-down compromise -- it gets centralization's consistency where it actually matters platform-wide, and decentralization's speed where a change only affects one team.

questions.q: What does 'blast radius' mean in this lesson, and how is it used in the centralization-vs-decentralization decision?
options: The number of users licensed in an org
The amount of API calls consumed by a single integration

How much of the org is affected if a given change goes wrong -- changes to shared, foundational elements carry a larger blast radius that justifies central review, while team-scoped changes carry a smaller one that's a reasonable candidate for decentralized authority
The size of a Salesforce Shield encryption key
questions.explain: Blast radius is the lesson's criterion for deciding which changes need central review (high blast radius, shared/foundational elements) versus which are safe to decentralize (low blast radius, team-scoped changes).

questions.q: Per this lesson, what does the one-org-vs-multi-org decision trade off, at the level of overall Salesforce architecture?
options: Salesforce does not support running more than one org per company
Multiple orgs are always cheaper than one shared org regardless of team count
One shared org eliminates the need for any Center of Excellence model

One shared org gives a common data model and strong cross-team reporting at the cost of needing governance discipline; multiple orgs give full business-unit autonomy at the cost of duplicated licensing and real integration work to share data
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly extends the centralization-vs-decentralization tension up to the org-architecture level: one org centralizes the data model and reporting at a governance cost, while multiple orgs decentralize autonomy at a licensing and integration cost.
